relationship: Renewed covenant demand
rationale: The command to love the Lord and keep His charges resumes the preceding demand to love, serve and keep His commandments for Israel's good.

relationship: Same-chapter eyewitness framing
rationale: Moses distinguishes his hearers from children without these experiences; the later statement specifies that the hearers' own eyes saw the Lord's great works.

relationship: Historical recital and announced Egyptian signs
rationale: The recital names signs against Pharaoh and Egypt; Exodus announces multiplied signs and judgments by which Egypt will know the Lord when Israel departs.

relationship: Historical recital and sea-deliverance account
rationale: Moses recalls the destruction of Egypt's horsemen and chariots by the sea; Exodus describes returning waters covering the pursuing chariots, horsemen and army.

relationship: Same-chapter wilderness recital and particular example
rationale: The summary of the Lord's wilderness deeds is followed by the specific judgment on Dathan and Abiram, whose households and tents the earth swallowed.

relationship: Historical recital and named wilderness judgment
rationale: Both identify Dathan and Abiram and describe the earth opening to swallow their households and possessions; Numbers supplies the immediate narrative surrounding this judgment.

relationship: Same-chapter eyewitness framing
rationale: The affirmation that the hearers' own eyes saw these deeds answers the earlier distinction between these hearers and children who had not known or seen them.

relationship: Obedience linked with entry and possession
rationale: Both urge Israel to keep the delivered ordinances so that the people may enter and inherit the promised land; chapter4 also explicitly connects this with living.

relationship: Promised land, ancestral pledge and obedient prosperity
rationale: Both connect heeding instruction with the land flowing with milk and honey, while invoking the Lord's pledge to the fathers and promised wellbeing there.

relationship: Same-chapter contrasting water supplies
rationale: Egypt's seed and watering with the feet are contrasted with the coming land's hills and plains drinking heaven's rain; no particular irrigation device is identified.

relationship: Same-chapter contrasting water supplies
rationale: The land watered by rain from heaven is explicitly contrasted with Egypt's sowing and watering with the feet, preserving the two descriptions without importing a mechanism.

relationship: Same-chapter divine care and specified provision
rationale: The land under the Lord's eyes throughout the year receives specified rain, crops and cattle grass in the following conditional promise; the descriptions of care and obedience remain distinct.

relationship: Wholehearted love in covenant instruction
rationale: Both require love for the Lord with the whole heart and soul; this passage additionally states hearkening to commands and serving Him in that wholehearted manner.

relationship: Parallel obedience-and-rain promises
rationale: Both connect keeping divine instruction with seasonal rain and agricultural yield; Deuteronomy specifies early and latter rain together with grain, wine and oil.

relationship: Same-chapter complementary agricultural provisions
rationale: Grass for cattle and human fullness complete the preceding rain-and-crop promise, distinguishing pasture for livestock from the named grain, wine and oil harvests.

relationship: Warning against other gods and divine wrath
rationale: Both warn Israel against turning to other gods; the earlier passage expressly connects this with the Lord's jealousy and anger, developed here by the following drought warning.

relationship: Parallel covenant drought warnings
rationale: The closed heaven and withheld rain correspond to the later curse describing bronze heaven, iron earth and dust instead of rain, without equating their distinct imagery.

relationship: Repeated heart, hand and eye instruction
rationale: Both place these words in the heart and soul and bind them as a hand sign and something immovable before the eyes, preserving the repeated household-remembrance instruction.

relationship: Repeated settings for teaching children
rationale: Both command teaching the words to children while sitting at home, walking on the road, lying down and rising, giving the same recurring daily occasions.

relationship: Repeated written household reminder
rationale: Both command writing the words on the doorposts of houses and on gates, preserving a particular household and communal location for remembrance.

relationship: Obedience and lengthened generations in the land
rationale: The promise of multiplied days for the hearers and children corresponds to the earlier instruction concerning hearers, sons and sons' sons, with prolonged days as its stated purpose.

relationship: Repeated love, walking and command-keeping
rationale: Both combine loving the Lord, walking in His ways and keeping His instruction; this verse's cleaving language is retained without treating the two lists as identical.

relationship: Expulsion of stronger nations
rationale: Both describe the Lord handing over or driving out nations before Israel, explicitly calling those nations stronger or greater than the receiving people.

relationship: Promised territory and footsole formula
rationale: Both promise the territory trodden by the feet and name Anti-Lebanon, the Euphrates and western sea among the boundaries, preserving this edition's geographical wording.

relationship: Related assurances that opponents cannot withstand
rationale: The assurance to Israel that no one will withstand them corresponds to the assurance addressed personally to Joshua; the different recipients and accompanying language remain distinct.

relationship: Blessing-and-curse announcement and later law reading
rationale: Moses sets blessing and curse before Israel; the actual Joshua continuation unit records the reading of all the law's words, including its blessings and curses.

relationship: Conditional blessing and developed blessing list
rationale: Blessing is conditioned on hearkening to the Lord's commands; the later chapter introduces the same condition and specifies blessings upon city, field, offspring and daily movements.

relationship: Conditional curse and developed curse list
rationale: Failure to hearken brings the announced curse; the later chapter develops curses upon city, field, offspring and movements, while this verse specifically also mentions other gods.

relationship: Mountain assignment and later tribal arrangement
rationale: Gerizim is assigned blessing and Ebal curse; the later instruction names the tribes standing upon each mountain for those respective declarations.

relationship: Mountain command and subsequent ceremony
rationale: The later Joshua unit places halves of Israel near Gerizim and Ebal with the ark and officials, expressly relating the arrangement to Moses' prior blessing command.

relationship: Same-chapter location of the specified mountains
rationale: The location beyond Jordan toward the west and adjoining Gilgal identifies the mountains just named for blessing and curse; the lofty oak receives no imported site identification.

relationship: Jordan crossing and inheritance instruction
rationale: Both announce crossing Jordan into the land given to Israel; Joshua receives the direct command to rise and lead the people across after Moses' death.

relationship: Transition into the detailed land ordinances
rationale: The requirement to perform the ordinances and judgments leads directly into the heading identifying ordinances and judgments to observe throughout life in the inherited land.

relationship: Same-chapter legal heading and specified commands
rationale: The heading about ordinances in the inherited land introduces particular instructions to destroy prior cult sites and bring gifts to the Lord's chosen place for rejoicing.

relationship: Parallel destruction of prior cult installations
rationale: Both require destruction of the nations' cult installations; this verse locates their worship on mountains, hills and under trees, while chapter7 specifies altars and other objects.

relationship: Repeated instructions against cult objects
rationale: Both enumerate altars, pillars, groves and carved images for destruction, with this verse also commanding removal of their names from that place.

relationship: Same-chapter negative and positive worship instruction
rationale: The prohibition against doing so to the Lord is followed by seeking His chosen place and name; the link preserves the stated contrast without resolving every possible antecedent.

relationship: Chosen place and later explicit Jerusalem testimony
rationale: Deuteronomy commands seeking the place chosen for the Lord's name without naming it; the later testimony explicitly identifies Jerusalem as the chosen city for that name.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated destination for offerings
rationale: Both direct listed offerings and gifts to the place chosen for the Lord's name, though their particular lists and descriptions are not identical.

relationship: Rejoicing before the Lord with the household
rationale: Both associate rejoicing with the Lord's chosen place and household participation; the festival instruction additionally enumerates Levites, sojourners, orphans and widows.

relationship: Same-chapter present practice and coming settlement
rationale: The prohibition on continuing each person's present practice is explained by the lack of rest and inheritance, followed by settlement and the chosen offering place.

relationship: Awaited land and rest and later settlement summary
rationale: The rest and inheritance not yet reached are later described as land given to Israel with rest around them and the fulfillment of the Lord's good word.

relationship: Promised rest from enemies and later narrative summary
rationale: The promised settlement and rest from surrounding enemies correspond to Joshua's statement that the Lord gave rest around Israel and delivered their enemies into their hands.

relationship: Same-chapter chosen destination for named gifts
rationale: The command to bring gifts to the chosen place resumes the earlier direction to seek that place and bring the named offerings there, preserving differences between the lists.

relationship: Levites' lack of territorial inheritance
rationale: The household rejoicing instruction includes the Levite because he has no allotment with Israel; Numbers similarly denies Levites an inheritance and assigns tithes for their service.

relationship: Related restrictions upon sacrificial location
rationale: Both reject offering sacrifices at an arbitrary location; Leviticus specifies the Tent entrance, while Deuteronomy's following instruction specifies the chosen place, without identifying the sites as one.

relationship: Same-chapter chosen-place exception to arbitrary sacrifice
rationale: The requirement to offer burnt offerings at the chosen place answers the immediately preceding prohibition against presenting them in every place one sees.

relationship: Same-chapter local meat permission repeated and qualified
rationale: Both permit local meat eating for clean and unclean persons using gazelle and deer comparisons; the later instruction additionally addresses enlarged territory and distance from the chosen place.

relationship: Parallel blood-pouring instructions with distinct details
rationale: Both require blood to be poured onto earth; Deuteronomy compares it with water, while Leviticus adds earth covering in its instruction concerning hunted animals and birds.

relationship: Same-chapter forbidden local consumption and required destination
rationale: The prohibition on eating specified tithes and gifts within the cities is answered by eating before the Lord in His chosen place with the named participants.

relationship: Same-chapter required destination for restricted foods
rationale: Eating these gifts before the Lord at the chosen place is contrasted with the preceding prohibition on city consumption; this verse's household and sojourner wording is retained.

relationship: Levite's inclusion and the warning against neglect
rationale: The warning not to forsake the Levite corresponds to his inclusion in the later household meal, where his lack of portion and inheritance is explicitly stated.

relationship: Same-chapter expanded-territory meat permission and implementation
rationale: The permission to eat desired meat after territorial enlargement is developed through distance from the chosen place, local slaughter and shared clean-and-unclean eating.

relationship: Different stated slaughter regulations
rationale: Deuteronomy permits local cattle and sheep slaughter when the chosen place is distant; Leviticus requires bringing the named slaughtered animals to the Tent entrance, preserving the differing instructions.

relationship: Related local clean-and-unclean meal rules
rationale: Both compare local meat eating with gazelle and deer and allow clean and unclean persons; chapter15 applies this to a blemished firstborn and separately prohibits blood.

relationship: Blood prohibition grounded in life
rationale: Both connect blood with life and forbid its consumption; Leviticus additionally states its assigned altar role and gives particular handling instructions for hunted animals.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated blood disposal formula
rationale: Both prohibit consuming blood and command pouring it onto the earth like water, repeating the particular prohibition alongside the chapter's meat permissions.

relationship: Same-chapter wellbeing attached to the blood prohibition
rationale: The promise of wellbeing for the hearer and children follows the explicit command not to consume blood and to pour it upon the earth.

relationship: Same-chapter holy gifts distinguished from ordinary local meat
rationale: Holy things and vows must be carried to the chosen place, whereas the earlier permission allows distant local slaughter and clean-and-unclean eating of ordinary meat.

relationship: Related altar treatment with different specifications
rationale: Both direct sacrificial blood to the Lord's altar; Deuteronomy describes its base and flesh instructions, while Leviticus specifies blood around the altar and fat upon it.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated intergenerational wellbeing formula
rationale: Both connect doing what is right before the Lord with wellbeing for the hearer and descendants; verse28 extends the admonition to all these words.

relationship: Dispossession preceding Israel's occupation
rationale: Both describe the Lord removing or delivering the nations before Israel's entry and possession, setting the following cult warnings within that anticipated occupation.

relationship: Same-chapter imitation warning and specified abomination
rationale: The warning against asking how the nations served their gods is followed by the particular example of sons and daughters burned for those gods.

relationship: Prohibited child-burning and later prophetic condemnation
rationale: Deuteronomy condemns burning sons and daughters for gods; Jeremiah condemns burning sons and daughters at Topheth and says this was neither commanded nor conceived by the Lord.

relationship: Repeated prohibition on adding or removing words
rationale: Both prohibit adding to or taking away from the commanded words, preserving this edition's placement at13:1 rather than substituting a different chapter division.

relationship: Same-chapter prophet-sign case and response
rationale: The introduction of a prophet or dreamer offering a sign is developed by the sign's occurrence, enticement to other gods and the command not to listen.

relationship: Different prophetic tests
rationale: Here a fulfilled sign accompanies enticement to other gods and must be rejected; chapter18 also addresses other-god speech and distinguishes a prediction that does not occur.

relationship: Testing the heart in distinct circumstances
rationale: Both describe divine testing to reveal the heart's response; the wilderness account concerns humbled dependence and command keeping, while this passage tests wholehearted love amid religious enticement.

relationship: Repeated exclusive devotion instructions
rationale: Both command fearing the Lord and remaining joined or cleaving to Him; chapter13 adds walking and heeding His voice, while chapter10 names service and swearing by His name.

relationship: Parallel death judgments for other-god prophetic speech
rationale: Both prescribe death in a case involving prophetic speech for other gods; chapter13 also names the dreamer and grounds the offense in turning Israel from its deliverer.

relationship: Same-chapter intimate enticement case and prescribed response
rationale: The enticement by a brother, child, wife or close friend receives a particular response of refusing consent, reporting and the stated communal judgment procedure.

relationship: Same-chapter scope of the enticer's proposed gods
rationale: The surrounding nations' gods, whether near or distant, continue the preceding private invitation to worship gods unknown to the hearer and ancestors.

relationship: Same-chapter refusal followed by reporting and judgment
rationale: The prohibitions on consent, listening, pity and concealment are followed by reporting, first-hand participation and communal stoning; the source's reporting wording is preserved.

relationship: Initial hands and subsequent communal participation
rationale: Both put particular hands first before those of all the people in execution; chapter17 specifically identifies witnesses, whereas this case addresses the person being enticed.

relationship: Same-chapter stated reason for the enticer's judgment
rationale: Stoning is grounded in the attempted turning from the Lord who brought Israel from Egypt; the preceding verses define the private enticement and required response.

relationship: Communal hearing and fear as deterrence
rationale: Both conclude a prescribed death judgment with Israel hearing and fearing so that the offense is not repeated; chapter17 concerns defiance of priestly or judicial authority.

relationship: Same-chapter reported city offense and following process
rationale: A report about a city given for dwelling is developed into the charge of enticement, diligent investigation and judgment only after the allegation is established.

relationship: Same-chapter city allegation requiring investigation
rationale: The allegation that lawless men led a city's inhabitants after other gods is immediately followed by searching, inquiry and verification that the alleged abomination is true.

relationship: Parallel investigation before idolatry judgment
rationale: Both require careful inquiry and confirmation of an alleged abomination before judgment; chapter17 adds witness requirements for the individual case rather than this city-wide case.

relationship: Same-chapter city judgment conditioned on verified charge
rationale: The prescribed destruction of the city follows the specific allegation of other-god enticement and the requirement to establish its truth through diligent investigation.

relationship: Related city-burning and non-rebuilding language
rationale: Both describe burning a city and language against rebuilding; Joshua concerns Jericho, includes metal-treasure exceptions and a builder's curse, rather than this law's proven apostate city.

relationship: Devoted property barred from private appropriation
rationale: Both warn against taking devoted property; Joshua separately assigns specified metals to the Lord's treasury, whereas Deuteronomy's preceding city instruction burns its spoil.

relationship: Same-chapter obedience concluding the testing-and-allegiance frame
rationale: The closing condition of hearing, keeping commands and doing right returns to the earlier test of wholehearted love and command to follow, heed and cleave to the Lord.

relationship: Related mourning baldness prohibitions with different addressees
rationale: Deuteronomy addresses the Lord's children and prohibits purification rites and a bald place for the dead; Leviticus' priestly instruction includes the particular mourning bald-patch prohibition.

relationship: Repeated holy and chosen possession description
rationale: Both describe Israel as holy to the Lord and chosen from the peoples as His possession, providing the stated communal identity behind the surrounding instructions.

relationship: Dietary prohibition and clean-unclean discrimination
rationale: The prohibition on eating abominations introduces a food list; Leviticus closes its animal law by distinguishing clean from unclean and edible from inedible creatures.

relationship: Same-chapter named permitted livestock and qualifying criteria
rationale: The permitted calf, sheep and goat list is followed by the split-hoof and cud-chewing criteria for eating beasts, linking the named livestock with the stated food rule.

relationship: Same-chapter named wild animals and stated food criteria
rationale: The named wild-animal list precedes the split-hoof and cud-chewing criterion; the connection does not adjudicate the modern zoological identities of bubalos, goat-stag, oryx or giraffe.

relationship: Parallel split-hoof and cud-chewing criteria
rationale: Both permit eating beasts that divide the hoof and chew the cud, stating the two traits together rather than treating either trait alone as sufficient.

relationship: Parallel exceptions to the two-trait rule
rationale: Both exclude named cud-chewing animals that lack divided hooves and share camel and hare examples; rock-hyrax and choirogryllios wording is preserved without asserting name equivalence.

relationship: Parallel pig and carcass prohibitions
rationale: Both exclude the pig because its divided hoof is not accompanied by cud chewing and prohibit eating its flesh and touching the specified carcasses.

relationship: Parallel aquatic food criteria
rationale: Both allow water creatures possessing fins and scales, joining the same two characteristics as the condition for eating them.

relationship: Parallel exclusion of aquatic creatures lacking criteria
rationale: Both exclude water creatures lacking fins and scales; Leviticus develops the prohibition with abomination language and flesh-and-carcass instructions.

relationship: Same-chapter clean-flying-creature permissions framing exclusions
rationale: The clean-bird permission before the prohibited list corresponds to the clean-flying-creature permission after it, preserving the source's differing terms rather than claiming identical wording.

relationship: Parallel prohibited-bird list opening with preserved names
rationale: Both open the forbidden-bird examples with eagle and sea-eagle; Deuteronomy's griffon-vulture and Leviticus' gryps forms remain distinct without a zoological identification claim.

relationship: Parallel vulture-and-kite exclusion
rationale: Both prohibit the vulture and kite with the accompanying kind-language, giving a specific shared element of the two prohibited-bird lists.

relationship: Parallel raven-kind exclusion
rationale: Both exclude the raven and its like, retaining a particular shared list entry rather than a general resemblance between food laws.

relationship: Parallel ostrich, owl and gull list entries
rationale: Both list ostrich, owl and gull among the forbidden creatures; Leviticus also places the hawk in this unit, preserving the differing grouping.

relationship: Parallel prohibited names distributed across different units
rationale: Deuteronomy groups heron, swan and ibis together; Leviticus includes these names across several units, so the comparison does not impose identical list positions.

relationship: Parallel prohibited names with different list grouping
rationale: The diving bird, hawk, hoopoe and night-raven appear within Leviticus' longer grouping as well; the actual unit boundaries and order are preserved rather than aligned artificially.

relationship: Parallel pelican, plover and bat entries with preserved names
rationale: Both passages include pelican, plover and bat; Deuteronomy's purple-swamphen and Leviticus' purple-waterbird wording remains distinct without claiming a modern species equivalence.

relationship: Related creeping-flying prohibition with stated exceptions in Leviticus
rationale: Both restrict creeping flying creatures; Leviticus additionally permits specified leaping kinds, a qualification retained rather than silently added to Deuteronomy's shorter prohibition.

relationship: Same-chapter clean-creature permissions around the prohibited list
rationale: The clean-flying-creature permission closes the list introduced after the clean-bird permission, preserving their particular terms without treating them as identical sentences.

relationship: Different dead-animal food instructions
rationale: Deuteronomy forbids Israel to eat an animal dead of itself and permits transfer to aliens or foreigners; Leviticus describes washing and impurity after native or alien consumption.

relationship: Repeated prohibition concerning a lamb in its mother's milk
rationale: Both forbid boiling a lamb in its mother's milk; the adjacent instructions differ, with Exodus naming firstfruits and Deuteronomy discussing dead-animal food and holy identity.

relationship: Related seed-and-produce tithe instructions
rationale: Deuteronomy specifies an annual tithe of field produce; Leviticus declares the land's seed and fruit tithe holy to the Lord without stating that annual timing in this verse.

relationship: Chosen-place consumption of restricted gifts
rationale: Both direct consumption of specified tithes and firstborn gifts before the Lord at His chosen place; chapter12 explicitly contrasts prohibited city consumption and lists participants.

relationship: Same-chapter distance condition and silver provision
rationale: When distance prevents carrying the gifts, the following instructions allow conversion to silver, transport to the chosen place and purchase for the household meal.

relationship: Same-chapter silver transport linked to inability to carry
rationale: The command to convert into silver and travel to the chosen place answers the preceding condition of distance and inability to carry what the Lord has blessed.

relationship: Same-chapter chosen-place spending after silver conversion
rationale: Spending on cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink and desired food implements the preceding distant-carriage provision, followed here by household eating and rejoicing before the Lord.

relationship: Levite's lack of inheritance grounds inclusion
rationale: Both connect care or inclusion of the Levite with his lack of portion and inheritance alongside Israel; chapter12 places him within rejoicing at the chosen place.

relationship: Third-year local tithe distribution with distinct descriptions
rationale: Both describe third-year provision for the Levite, sojourner, orphan and widow; chapter14 says all the tithe, whereas chapter26 calls it the second tithe, without harmonizing the descriptions.

relationship: Named four groups eating the third-year provision
rationale: Both name Levite, sojourner, orphan and widow receiving and eating the provision; chapter26 also includes the giver's declaration that the holy things have been distributed.
